experiment: SD read CRC16 check on/off with the UI quiet (ui_hz=0), chunk 128, 8 MiB, exFAT: what does KOS's CRC16 cost?

inputs.note: two complete bench runs in one saved log; the on-screen log wraps at 76 characters and was re-joined for parsing

config.note: the run's note= still said 'T1 ui census'; the OPTIONS lines are what ran

hardware.disc: Not named in the report. The TOC (tracks at FAD 150 / 1076 / 45150, lead-out 549300) matches Sword of the Berserk, as in t1-ui-census-2026-09-19.json.
hardware.note: CMD 24 FAILED sense=6/40 at the start of a run is the drive's first INIT after a disc change, not an error.

derived.method: check_crc governs only the read side (writes always compute and send a CRC16, and the card verifies it, CMD59). So the read-rate difference is the cost of KOS's net_crc16ccitt alone: cycles/byte = 200 MHz / (KiB/s x 1024).
conclusions: Turning the read CRC check off speeds SD reads by 8.3% (677.0 to 733.5 KiB/s) and leaves writes unchanged (-0.06%), as expected.

That difference is a direct measurement of KOS's CRC16 loop: 22.2 cycles a byte, 7.7% of an SD read. The write path runs the same function, so the same 22.2 cycles are 13.4% of an SD write (165.4 cycles a byte).

This agrees with the earlier estimate from Trip 1 (~21 cycles a byte) and with the instruction count of the compiled loop (28 instructions a byte at about 1.3 per cycle), so a faster CRC16 is the one SD-side change that recovers real time without weakening any check (Trip 1b measures the candidates).
Do not turn the read check off in the capture engine to gain this: it is the read-back's only wire-level protection. The gain is available from a faster function, not a weaker check.

limitations: One card, one disc, one console; two runs.
Run-to-run spread of the four rates is at most 0.2%.
